description: Hello everyone! I'm Afras - Full-Stack Engineer. Currently 2nd year CS Undergraduate at IIT Sri Lanka.
summary:
LunaScope is a screening tool that shows when the Sun and Earth are visible from sites near the Moon’s south pole. At the pole the Sun and Earth stay within a few degrees of the horizon, so a ridge a few kilometres away can hide them even when they are above a flat horizon. A flat-horizon estimate therefore overstates sunlight and the line of sight to Earth.

We built an interactive Moon atlas on real data. The terrain comes from LRO LOLA elevation models, and the Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons, checked against NAIF SPICE. For each site it computes a terrain-aware skyline and shows the Sun and Earth over it in a 3D “Site sky”, a timeline of exactly when each is hidden, and the evidence behind every number.

The tool follows three rules: nothing synthetic is shown as science, unknown is never counted as “not visible”, and there is no hidden combined score. Every result carries a trust label. It is a screening and education tool, not a landing-safety or mission-feasibility assessment, and it is not endorsed by NASA.
details:
WHAT LUNASCOPE IS

LunaScope is an interactive atlas of the Moon’s south pole that answers one question: at this site, on these dates, is the Sun or Earth above the terrain skyline? Near the pole both stay within a few degrees of the horizon, so a ridge a few kilometres away can hide them even when they are “above the horizon” on paper. A flat-horizon estimate therefore overstates sunlight and the line of sight to Earth. LunaScope computes the real terrain skyline and compares the Sun and Earth against it, over a mission window.

TRY IT IN 60 SECONDS

  1. Open the link. The Moon fills the screen, lit by the Sun.
  2. Pick a site in the Sites list (for example Shackleton) and press “Open GR-003”.
  3. Press “Site sky”, look around, then press Play on the time dock.
  4. Open Timeline and Metrics to see when each target is hidden.

HOW THE SCIENCE WORKS

  1. Terrain skyline. For a site we cast rays outward in every direction every 0.5° of azimuth, out to 150 km, over the 20 m LRO LOLA elevation model. Along each ray we sample the terrain (steps start at half a pixel near the site and grow slowly with distance) and take the largest elevation angle seen from the observer, with the Moon’s curvature included. That maximum is the skyline in that direction. Missing terrain data is treated as unknown, never as flat: a direction with gaps is marked “coverage limited” unless it provably cannot raise the skyline.
  2. Where the Sun and Earth are. Directions come from JPL Horizons. We convert them to the site’s local east, north and up frame and interpolate smoothly between samples (cubic Hermite). An independent geometry check uses NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440).
  3. Clearance. At every moment: clearance = target elevation − skyline at the target’s azimuth. The target counts as visible when this is above zero. The centre of the Sun and of Earth is the default; a separate sensitivity case brackets the result using the real disc sizes (about 0.5° for the Sun and about 1.9° for Earth): “any part of the disc visible” and “whole disc visible”.
  4. Events and intervals. The window is split into visible, hidden, unknown and uncertified intervals. Rise and set times are found by root-finding, but only on stretches where bounds prove there is exactly one crossing. Anything that can’t be proven is reported as uncertified, never as “no event”.
  5. Metrics. Durations, not sample counts: availability (shown as a lower and upper bound), longest hidden period, total hidden time, best clearance. Stated requirements, such as a minimum availability, pass or fail separately for the Sun and for Earth. They are never combined.
  6. Validation and evidence. A second skyline is computed a different way (pixel-driven from the raw DEM, with different geometry code) and must agree within set tolerances. Every run carries provenance, resource hashes, sensitivity variants (for example a halved azimuth step) and an export bundle whose hash can be checked. Results are “real data, unverified”: no validation gate has closed.
  7. Time Machine and dates search. A mission window can be shifted by days and compared with the original, and a search runs several start dates, so you see how sensitive a site is to timing.

HOW EACH FEATURE WORKS

  1. The Moon. NASA’s LRO wide-angle camera mosaic, streamed from NASA Moon Trek, lit from the Sun’s real position at the clock time (a display estimate good to about a degree): the sunlit half is bright and the other half dark, and the boundary moves as time runs.
  2. Sites. Every catalogue site is a pin: three rule-chosen demonstration points at 89.5°S and twelve IAU-named places (the Artemis III candidate-region features and well-known shadowed craters). A solid ring means the terrain data covers the site’s whole 150 km footprint. These are named places, not landing recommendations.
  3. Time dock. Play and pause, five speeds (1 minute to 1 day per second), reverse, loop, previous and next event, a scrubber and Go to (UTC). The browser only picks and interpolates what the service computed.
  4. Site sky (3D). The ground is built from real LOLA heights (a 25 km patch at 150 m spacing, with curvature) and the service’s skyline stands beyond it. The Sun and Earth are where the data puts them at the clock time, the Earth picture turns with real time, and heights can be exaggerated (always stated on screen). Ground shading is illustrative, with no cast shadows.
  5. Timeline. Sun and Earth bars over the window, rise and set ticks, the flat-horizon result beside the terrain result, a table and a CSV export.
  6. Metrics, Clearance, Sky path, Compare, Dates, Evidence, Analyse, Runs, Learn. Numbers, margins over the skyline, flat sky plots, site comparison, date shifts, the evidence bundle, a form to set up your own analysis, saved runs and an explainer with key terms. Press Ctrl+K to search.
  7. Interface. Panels drag and resize on a wide screen and become bottom sheets on a phone. It works with the keyboard and was tested with automated accessibility checks.

TECHNOLOGY: HOW IT’S BUILT

  • Web app: Next.js (App Router), React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI. CesiumJS draws the Moon globe and three.js draws the Site sky; both load only when needed. The browser never decides visibility: it displays the service’s results.
  • Science service: Python with FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj and SpiceyPy. Runs go through a job queue with a worker (at most two at once, with a per-run time limit) and are stored in SQLite with content-addressed result files. A run’s ID is a hash of its request, settings and resources, so identical inputs give the same run.
  • API contract: the API is described by an OpenAPI file, and the web app’s types are generated from it and checked for drift.
  • Safe proxy: the browser talks only to our own /api/v1 proxy, which allows a fixed list of routes and rebuilds the upstream address from validated parts, so a request can’t be steered elsewhere.
  • Replay mode: the hosted copy serves saved real-data runs from a package whose files are hash-checked offline; it refuses anything not saved, with a clear message.
  • Quality: hundreds of unit tests (web and Python), Playwright end-to-end tests and axe accessibility checks. Hosted on Vercel (web) and Render (service).

WHAT MAKES IT TRUSTWORTHY

Three rules are built in: no placeholder is shown as science, unknown is never counted as “not visible”, and there is no hidden combined score. Every block carries a trust label (NASA data, derived, assumption, illustration, synthetic, replay).

DATA

LRO LOLA 20 m elevation models (NASA PGDA and PDS), JPL Horizons ephemerides checked against NAIF SPICE, NASA Moon Trek imagery, and NASA Blue Marble and SDO pictures.

LIMITS, STATED PLAINLY

This is a screening and education tool, not a landing-safety, power, link-budget or mission-feasibility assessment. The Sun and Earth are treated as their centres by default, with disc sensitivity reported separately. The skyline is converged under the tested settings, not a proof that every obstacle is resolved. The hosted copy shows saved reference runs (GR-001, GR-002 and GR-003) and cannot compute new points. To analyse your own sites and dates, run it locally: https://github.com/MohamedAfrasDev/LunaScope/blob/main/docs/RUN-LOCALLY.md. Not endorsed by NASA.
